kept.corrected_quote: There was a man of Sung, who was grieved that his growing corn was not longer, and so he pulled it up. ... 'I have been helping the corn to grow long.' His son ran to look at it, and found the corn all withered.
kept.corrected_meaning: He pulled his young plants up to help them grow faster. Soon they had all dried up.
kept.evidence: I downloaded the archive.org full text of Legge's The Four Books (Commercial Press reprint, item fourbooksconfuci00leggiala, undated) and checked the headings: 'BOOK II, KUNG-SUN CH'OW. PART I', then 'CHAPTER II', then para. 16. It reads: 'There was a man of Sung, who was grieved that his growing corn was not longer, and so he pulled it up. Having done this, he returned home, looking very stupid, and said to his people, 'I am tired to-day. I have been helping the corn to grow long.' His son ran to look at it, and found the corn all withered.' The quoted words match exactly. The trim is marked and only removes 'Having done this... I am tired to-day.' I only tidied the punctuation at the cut ('up. ...'). The follow-up line in the notes is also exact: 'Some indeed consider it of no benefit to them, and let it alone:-- they do not weed their corn. They who assist it to grow long, pull out their corn.' Fix needed in the meaning line: the text never says 'next morning'. The son runs out to look the same day, right after the man says 'I am tired to-day'. The attribution, chapter and translator are correct. This is not in used_quotes.txt. The only Mencius entries there are 'Heaven is about to confer a great office' and 'intelligent virtue and prudence'.
kept.safety: Safe. It is a farming parable. The man is from the state of Sung (Song), named only as his home, with nothing political about it. The trim removes 'looking very stupid', so nobody is mocked. No war, royalty, disaster, crime or old-age content.

kept.corrected_meaning: Do not rush, and do not chase small wins. Rushing stops a job from being done well.
kept.evidence: I checked two sources. (1) Project Gutenberg #4094, Legge, The Chinese Classics Vol. 1: Confucian Analects, at CHAP. XVII. The Master said, 'Do not be desirous to have things done quickly; do not look at small advantages. Desire to have things done quickly prevents their being done thoroughly. Looking at small advantages prevents great affairs from being accomplished.'' (2) The Commercial Press Four Books scan on archive.org has the same wording in CHAPTER XVII. The quote matches word for word, as a clean cut that ends after 'thoroughly.'. The number 13.17 and Legge 1861 are correct. This is the source of the idiom 欲速则不达. It is not misattributed, and it is not in used_quotes.txt (the only Confucius entries there are 9.19 basketful, 'one effort... a hundred efforts', and 'At fifteen'). My meaning line is slightly better than the original because it also covers 'small advantages'. The original meaning, 'If you rush to finish, you never finish it well', is also acceptable. I also checked the extra idea, Mencius 6A18: it does read 'as if with one cup of water they could save a whole' cartload of fuel on fire, and later 'water cannot subdue fire'.
kept.safety: Safe as quoted. The setting is political: a disciple who has just become a town governor asks about government. Leave the setting off the slide and attribute it only as 'Confucius, Analects 13.17'. Do not add the last sentence about 'great affairs'. No war, royalty, disaster, crime or old-age content.

kept.corrected_quote: 石の上にも三年 / Three years, even on a stone.
kept.corrected_meaning: Sit on a cold stone long enough and it warms. Stay with hard things and they get easier.
kept.evidence: I fetched kotobank.jp/word/石の上にも三年-431901. Seisen-ban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten gives: '(冷たい石の上でも三年すわり続ければ暖まるの意から) たとえつらくてもしんぼう強くがんばれば、やがて報われるということ。〔俳諧・毛吹草（1638）〕'. Its first-use example is from Saikaku Oridome (1694): '商人、職人によらず、住なれたる所を替る事なかれ。石の上にも三年と俗言に伝へし' ('Merchant or craftsman, do not leave the place you are used to; as the saying goes, three years even on a stone'). That makes it a strong Side A line. Digital Daijisen and Kotowaza o Shiru Jiten give the same cold-stone-grows-warm gloss. Kotowaza o Shiru Jiten adds that the early Edo form was 石の上にも三年いれば温まる and was shortened from the late 17th century on. So the Japanese text and the dates are confirmed. The problem is the English. 'Even a cold stone grows warm if you sit on it three years' is the dictionaries' explanation, not a translation of 石の上にも三年. 'Cold', 'warm' and 'sit' are not in the short form printed next to it. The literal sense is 'Three years, even on a stone', and Wikiquote cites a published rendering '[To stay] three years on a rock' (Lee & Nadeau, Encyclopedia of Asian American Folklore and Folklife, ABC-CLIO 2011, p. 636), though I could not open that page to confirm it. My fix keeps the short form with a true literal English line and moves the warmth idea into the meaning line. If you want the warmth on the slide itself, use the early Edo full form instead: 石の上にも三年いれば温まる / 'Sit on a stone three years and it grows warm' (labelled as the old full form, literal translation). The proverb is not in used_quotes.txt; Ovid's stone line there is a different quote.
